ETF tracking: the gap between the index and your return

Use four charts to compare matched NAV and index returns, separate annual and cumulative gaps, and distinguish tracking difference from tracking error.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare matched hypothetical NAV and benchmark returns

Interactive planning lab

Ending hypothetical fund NAV wealth$21,036.01
Fund minus benchmark ending wealth-$553.24
Repeated annual fund-minus-benchmark return gap-0.28 pp

All fund names, benchmark returns, return gaps and attribution entries are invented. The fund and benchmark use the same opening CAD value, dates, currency and total-return basis with distributions reinvested. The annual fund NAV return equals the benchmark assumption plus the entered percentage-point gap, which can have either sign. It is already net of any costs reflected in that assumed NAV return: no second expense-ratio deduction is made. Annual factors repeat without contributions, withdrawals or probabilities. The benchmark wealth line is a calculation reference, not a directly purchasable investment. No investor tax, brokerage charges, spread, premium/discount or FX conversion is included. The separate four-month sample and attribution bridge remain fixed original illustrations; they do not generate the selected annual gap. These figures do not estimate a real fund’s tracking error or future performance.

The central idea

Compare the exact benchmark with fund NAV total return first. Then account for the price, spread and conversion costs of your own transaction.

01

Keep three return records separate

An index return describes a calculation maintained by an index provider. A fund’s NAV total return describes the performance of its net assets with the stated distribution-reinvestment convention. Your account return additionally reflects the prices and dates of your trades, your cash flows, and any investor-level costs.

Write all three on separate lines. Comparing your brokerage account gain with a headline price index can mix distributions, purchase timing, and fund implementation in one unexplained difference. A reliable comparison starts with matching dates, currency, benchmark version, and return definition.

The CFA Institute’s ETF overview discusses tracking, trading costs, and premiums or discounts. Those are related dimensions, but they require different measurements.

02

Tracking difference measures the return gap

On this page, tracking difference means fund NAV total return minus benchmark total return over the same interval. Some publishers reverse the sign, so check the stated convention. If the benchmark returns 8.00% and the fund returns 7.72%, the difference is −0.28 percentage points, or −28 basis points.

Tracking difference = fund NAV total return − matching benchmark total return

Do not subtract the fund’s expense ratio again from a published return that is already net of those expenses. Doing so would charge the same cost twice. Similarly, if the benchmark has a net-dividend convention, do not assume the resulting gap is entirely caused by withholding tax.

For a multi-year comparison, state whether you subtract annualized returns or compare cumulative wealth. These produce different-looking numbers. An eight-year cumulative shortfall cannot be labelled an annual cost without a suitable annualization.

Vanguard Canada’s index-tracking explanation uses this fund-minus-index convention and distinguishes the gap from its standard-deviation measure. The OSC Investor Office’s ETF Facts sample describes displayed performance as net of expenses, supporting the check against deducting an embedded expense twice. Read the actual return definition before applying that check to a real statement.

03

A small annual gap compounds into a different cumulative comparison

The controls start both references at CAD 10,000. The benchmark’s hypothetical annual total return is 8.00%, and the fund’s annual NAV total return is 7.72%. The annual fund-minus-benchmark tracking difference is therefore −0.28 percentage points. These are assumed net NAV results; no separate expense-ratio subtraction follows.

After ten identical annual factors, benchmark reference wealth is about CAD 21,589.25 and fund NAV wealth is about CAD 21,036.01. The signed fund-minus-benchmark wealth difference is approximately negative CAD 553.24. Relative to the same initial CAD 10,000, that is a −5.5324 percentage-point difference between the two cumulative returns.

That cumulative return gap is neither the annual −0.28 percentage-point gap nor the percentage by which ending fund wealth is below ending benchmark wealth. Each comparison uses a different denominator or horizon. Dividing −5.5324 by ten would not recover the annual rate difference.

The signed bars state each horizon explicitly. Changing the annual gap to a positive value lets the hypothetical fund exceed the benchmark; this is a sensitivity, not evidence that a real fund can repeatedly achieve that result. The benchmark wealth reference is also a calculation, rather than a directly investable account with no implementation costs.

04

Tracking error measures how variable the gap is

Tracking error is commonly the annualized standard deviation of periodic fund-minus-benchmark returns. It asks how much the gap fluctuates. It does not directly measure how much return the investor lost over the whole period.

Four invented monthly active returns · percentage points
MonthFund A minus indexFund B minus index
1−0.02+0.10
2−0.02−0.14
3−0.02+0.10
4−0.02−0.14

Both series have an arithmetic mean gap of −0.02 percentage points per month. Fund A has zero variability in this deliberately artificial sample; Fund B does not. This is a demonstration of the distinction, not enough history for a useful tracking-error estimate. Equal arithmetic mean gaps also do not guarantee equal compounded wealth.

In a real study, record daily or monthly frequency, the sample period, the standard-deviation convention, and the annualization factor. Compare like with like rather than ranking incompatible published statistics.

The monthly chart uses the exact four observations in this table, independent of the annual controls. The two artificial series have the same simple mean and different dispersion, but the page does not present their annualized standard deviations as useful estimates. A four-observation pattern illustrates a definition; it does not establish a fund’s likely future tracking error.

Do not compound the active-return differences by themselves to reconstruct fund wealth. You would also need the benchmark’s return for each matching month, then compound the fund and benchmark series separately. The monthly pattern and the annual wealth path are deliberately separate examples.

05

Build an explanation instead of guessing from the fee

Suppose a hypothetical one-year gap is −0.28 percentage points. An analyst’s illustrative reconciliation might assign −0.15 to operating expenses, −0.06 to portfolio trading, −0.08 to unrecovered taxes, +0.03 to net lending revenue, and −0.02 to other implementation effects. The sum is −0.28.

This is an invented attribution, not a claim that public reports reveal each component exactly. In actual research, label observed expenses separately from inferred residuals. Sampling, cash balances, valuation timing, index changes, and the treatment of corporate actions can also require investigation.

A one-year favorable residual is not automatically a repeatable skill. Read the fund’s reports, benchmark methodology, replication policy, and lending disclosures before extrapolating it. Avoid choosing a fund because of a tiny return advantage that cannot be explained or survives only over one chosen interval.

06

Your entry and exit add another layer

The SEC ETF bulletin explains that exchange prices can differ from NAV and that the bid–ask spread affects investor costs. These trading effects sit outside a clean NAV-to-index comparison.

Imagine an unchanged order book with a bid of 49.95 and ask of 50.05. Buying 200 units at the ask costs 10,010. An immediate sale at the bid returns 9,990, a loss of 20 before commissions. Relative to the 50 midpoint, the initial purchase costs 10 and the sale another 10. This full round-trip spread is 0.20% of the 10,000 midpoint value.

A limit order controls the worst price you accept, but it can remain unfilled. Compare the quote with current underlying-market conditions; yesterday’s closing NAV may be a poor intraday fair-value reference when the underlying market is closed or moving quickly.

The separate ETF bid–ask spread and order-cost guide diagrams investor execution cash. Those costs belong to your trade record. They must not be inserted into fund NAV tracking difference as though every investor incurred the same execution price or commission.

07

Read the four figures as two controlled and two fixed examples

The first two figures share the controls: they compare annual NAV and benchmark growth factors, then show their cumulative return differences at stated horizons. The final two figures retain the original article’s independent examples: four monthly active returns and a one-year attribution that sums to −0.28 percentage points.

A change to the annual-gap input does not rewrite the fixed monthly pattern or scale the invented attribution components. That would imply a relationship which the example has not established. Their purpose is to show the difference between a measured gap, its variation and a proposed explanation.

The attribution waterfall uses percentage points throughout. A positive lending-revenue entry offsets part of the negative entries; it is not a separate return to add again to the ending wealth line. Real disclosures may support some components better than others. Leave an unexplained residual visible instead of presenting an exact-looking invented explanation as measured evidence.

08

A comparison sheet that can be checked

  1. Identify the legal fund, exact share class, benchmark, and hedging policy.
  2. Compare fund NAV and matching benchmark total returns over identical periods.
  3. Record operating expenses and realized tracking differences without subtracting costs twice.
  4. Inspect spread, premium or discount history, brokerage charges, and currency-conversion costs.
  5. Check holdings, replication, lending, and the explanation for persistent residuals.

For a long holding period, a persistent annual gap can outweigh a modest one-time trading cost. For frequent transactions, spreads and commissions can matter much more. Estimate both using the intended behavior, and keep that estimate separate from the fund’s published performance record.
